title: Over Camps and Playgrounds Such as These
intro: Abu Tammam praises Abu Dulaf al-Qasim ibn Isa al-Ijli, recalling his counsel during al-Afshin’s campaign against Babak. At a deserted camp, the poet wants time to weep while his companion has the camels’ interests at heart. On reaching Abu Dulaf he finds courtyards so eager for guests they nearly ride out to meet them. He hopes to carry home enough of his host’s generosity to become a giver in his own right.

translation: Over camps and playgrounds such as these
the jealously guarded tears were given leave to run.
1.sharh: The apparent puzzle is how tears can be both guarded and flowing. The ruined camp marks the instant when the poet releases what he has long held back.

translation: I say to one whom parting has never stricken, who never lodged
the hidden ache of love between his breastbone and his ribs,
2.sharh: The companion is as untouched by parting as someone who has escaped an infection. He has never had to make room in his body for the lingering guest called love.

translation: “Help me scatter the gathering of my tears.
I see no prospect of their gathering together again.”
3.sharh: His tears have gathered behind his eyes while the people who occasion them are scattered. He asks for help breaking up the one gathering that remains in his power.

translation: At the camp that day all your reproach was my enemy,
until your ignorance became my companion.
4.sharh: The scolding feels hostile until he remembers who is doing it. The companion’s inexperience offers the lover one reason to bear it.

translation: You have no wish to mount me on good sense.
The good you sought was that of the riding camels.
5.sharh: The adviser offers him a figurative mount called good sense. What really concerns the man, in the poet’s view, is the management of the actual mounts.

translation: Leave me to longing and ride on. Love will travel
to my burning heart with flowing tears.
6.sharh: His friend can take the road and love can take its own. The near-identical sounds of the two commands to travel make their different destinations audible.

translation: Playground of my youth, who gave you over to decay
and made you the playground of east and south winds?
7.sharh: The site has kept its old name and lost its players. East and south winds now have the freedom of what used to be a human playground.

translation: Newborn calamities struck you and scattered
my loves among the young gazelles with swelling breasts.
8.sharh: The same word introduces fresh calamities and the young women he loved. The first set of maidens, as it were, drives away the second.

translation: Many a band of riders shares with its camels a cup
of travelling that no wine mixer’s hand prepared.
9.sharh: The bottle passes between human riders and their animals. What makes them reel is the road, served in a cup no vintner ever touched.

translation: Through night travel they have eaten away the camels’ withers,
and their own shapes now rise like withers on their backs.
10.sharh: The riders have consumed their mounts without taking a bite. As the flesh wastes away, the men’s own silhouettes supply the humps missing beneath them.

translation: Their course is steered by the rubbing post of eastern lands,
the propped palm of western lands when care comes upon him.
11.sharh: A proverb calls the trusted adviser a rubbing post and a laden palm held up by a prop. The poet gives his guide both titles and a whole compass over which to exercise them.

translation: In a gentle girl he sees the face of an avenger,
in a strong, hard-cheeked camel the brow of one returning home.
12.sharh: For a man bent on getting somewhere, a beauty can look like someone with a grievance against him. The ungainly camel, able to take him on, wears the welcoming face.

translation: It is as though he bears a grudge against every corner
of the earth, or longs for every corner.
13.sharh: Two opposite motives would produce exactly the same restless journey. Look behind the rider and he appears resentful, look ahead and he is in love.

translation: Once the pale camels bring me face to face with Abu Dulaf,
the ties between me and misfortune are severed.
14.sharh: Abu Dulaf finally gives the journey an endpoint. Separation, so painful in the opening, becomes desirable when hardship is what the poet can leave behind.

translation: There you meet generosity where its childhood amulets fell,
and glory wearing its locks long.
15.sharh: The amulets tied on a child fall away as it grows up. Generosity grew up here, and glory, given the long locks of a noble youth, is equally at home.

translation: His gifts all but go out of their minds
unless a petitioner’s voice charms them back.
16.sharh: Ordinarily it is the petitioner who longs to receive something. Here the gifts themselves suffer suspense and a request works on them like a healing incantation.

translation: When the thrill of honour stirs him, his gifts change
the names of wishes that had lied.
17.sharh: A disappointed hope in Arabic can be called a lying wish. Abu Dulaf need only grant it to make its old name inaccurate.

translation: The courtyards of his homes almost brighten with welcome
and ride out, longing, to every rider.
18.sharh: Even the open ground a guest would normally dismount upon is impatient. The courtyards almost become mounted hosts who can go and fetch him.

translation: When he goes forth at morning he sends his dearest possession
forth as a bride, even to the meanest suitor.
19.sharh: The feminine noun for a choice possession lets the poet dress it as a bride. No test of the suitor’s social standing holds up this wedding.

translation: To him the ugliest sight is a man returning
clothed by the hand he hoped in, in failure’s robe.
20.sharh: A departing guest might wear a ceremonial robe from his host. The disgrace here is that his only visible distinction should be disappointment.

translation: Lovelier than blossom opened by the east wind
is the white of gifts against the black of needs.
21.sharh: Gift and want become contrasting colours. The bit of white that appears at the centre of a dark need outshines a wind-opened flower.

translation: When Lujaym sets bridles on its horses, surrounded
by the sons of al-Hisn, born of noble women,
22.sharh: The patron’s larger tribal family appears at the moment the horses are bridled. The noble ancestry of the neighbouring fighters sets up a different sort of kinship in the next line.

translation: then death, swords and spears
are their nearest kin in terror’s hour.
23.sharh: The next set of relatives is death and the weapons in their hands. Under stress these prove more intimate than any family name.

translation: Armies that leave no man of overbearing pride
unscathed, yet strip no man who does not fight them.
24.sharh: Their violence has a stated limit. The verb for despoiling someone sounds like the word for fighting, but a non-combatant need not suffer either.

translation: They stretch out hands, defiant and protecting,
that strike with swords which judge and cut.
25.sharh: Two pairs of almost matching words distinguish resistance from protection and final judgement from a cutting edge. The repeated sounds carry quite different claims.

translation: When the horses cleave the dust of battle, they splinter
the fronts of long spears in the fronts of battalions.
26.sharh: Both spear shafts and battalions have “breasts” in the Arabic. Their fronts meet so violently that the shafts split.

translation: If Tamim ever boasts of its bow
and adds that to its established honours,
27.sharh: The famous bow was accepted as a tribal chief’s guarantee. Tamim can count the trust placed in it among its honours, but the conditional sentence leaves room for a rival claim.

translation: then at Dhu Qar your swords shook
the very thrones of those who held Hajib’s bow in pledge.
28.sharh: Hajib pledged the bow to the Persian king. Abu Dulaf’s Bakri forebears can answer Tamim by invoking a victory over the power that took the pledge.

translation: Such beauties of honour that, set beside them,
the beauties of other peoples look like flaws.
29.sharh: Only the comparison changes. Traits that would ordinarily count as virtues can look like defects when set beside the patron’s family.

translation: Their noble deeds press so high
they seem to have blood to avenge among the stars.
30.sharh: The stars give height a destination and a blood debt supplies urgency. The deeds seem unable to rest until they run their quarry down.

translation: Al-Afshin knows, the man through whom
the robe of kingship is kept from every grasping hand,
31.sharh: The general is called as a witness. In the image of kingship as a robe others might seize, the man who protects it has every reason to value good counsel.

translation: that when the affair turned pitch black and put on
dust clouds blowing into the very eyes of experience,
32.sharh: Darkness first obscures the crisis, then dust blinds experience itself. The person who can still see the consequences must offer more than routine expertise.

translation: you rose above it by judgement, until you showed him
the outcome there before his very eyes,
33.sharh: The answer to the previous bayt’s obscurity is a change of vantage point. Abu Dulaf sees over the crisis and brings the future into his commander’s field of vision.

translation: at Arshaq, when a cloud streamed down upon them,
sweeping along with long lances and lean thoroughbreds.
34.sharh: The cloud at Arshaq is a body of troops. Its load of lances and costly horses makes the metaphor visible as the cavalry sweeps forward.

translation: You drew two counsels for him, a sword and a blade,
each a piercing star in the darkness.
35.sharh: Judgement can be drawn as readily as a sword. Both shine by cutting through something, one through danger and one through uncertainty.

translation: When roused to meet a crisis, you bring to bear on it
instincts keener than the fine edges of swords.
36.sharh: The sharpest equipment he brings to a crisis is his own disposition. Sword edges provide a standard against which his natural powers can be felt.

translation: After that, your memory in the caliph’s heart
stands in for you, given pride of place.
37.sharh: The name of the ruler and the word for a deputy share a root. At court the memory of Abu Dulaf has become his own honoured representative.

translation: Should you forget, he remembers. Should an envier speak,
his words fall blunt. A distant home is near.
38.sharh: The subject changes from the patron to the caliph and back to the detractor. A memory that outlasts the first man’s forgetfulness can also blunt another man’s words.

translation: You are with him present and absent
at once, and away from him absent and present.
39.sharh: One person can occupy two different places, his actual dwelling and the caliph’s thoughts. The repeated reversals hold the two kinds of presence together.

translation: To you we bring home the far-grazing verse,
after it lingered in a meadow of marvellous meanings.
40.sharh: Verse returns at evening like a herd that has grazed at a distance. What nourished it out there was the slow work of finding its meanings.

translation: Rarities found familiar company in your courtyard,
in glory itself. They are strangers no longer.
41.sharh: A rare turn of phrase is also, in the Arabic, a stranger. In the patron’s courtyard its unusual claims find a glory great enough to make them feel at home.

translation: If poetry could run out, yours would have drained it,
so much have your basins gathered down the ages.
42.sharh: An ancestral house can collect praise over generations as a basin collects water. The quantity already gathered would have exhausted a finite art.

translation: But it is the rain of minds. Whenever
one bank of its clouds clears, more clouds follow.
43.sharh: The argument quietly changes the source of supply. Each new mind can raise another rain cloud over the same waiting basins.

translation: I tell my companions, “This is al-Qasim, through whom
generosity made its tangled paths plain.”
44.sharh: Al-Qasim’s name suggests someone who apportions or gives shares. His practice resolves a question about generosity more clearly than competing definitions can.

translation: I hope his gifts send my riding camels home
with me an ocean, my own gifts sought in turn.
45.sharh: The traveller wants to come back an ocean in his own right. His final wish is to occupy for someone else the place Abu Dulaf now occupies for him.

1.1.4.head: أَربُع
1.1.4.meaning: Former camp sites or dwelling places.

1.2.1.head: أُذيلَ
1.2.1.meaning: Was let go after being guarded.

2.1.2.head: قُرحان
2.1.2.meaning: Someone untouched by an affliction, here a stranger to the pain of parting.

2.1.6.head: أَضافَ
2.1.6.meaning: Lodge as a guest, here said of love.

2.2.1.head: رَسيس
2.2.1.meaning: A deep-seated or lingering trace of love.

2.2.5.head: التَّرائِب
2.2.5.meaning: The bones of the upper chest.

5.2.5.head: الرَّكائِب
5.2.5.meaning: Camels trained or kept as mounts.

6.2.4.head: السَّوارِب
6.2.4.meaning: Flowing or coursing, here of tears.

8.2.4.head: الكَواعِب
8.2.4.meaning: Young women whose breasts have begun to swell.

9.2.7.head: قاطِب
9.2.7.meaning: Someone who mixes wine with water for serving.

10.1.4.head: الغَوارِب
10.1.4.meaning: The withers of a camel, at the front of the hump.

11.1.3.head: جُذَيل
11.1.3.meaning: A small post on which camels rub themselves, proverbial for a dependable adviser.

11.2.4.head: عُذَيق
11.2.4.meaning: A little date palm, recalling the proverb about a laden tree supported by a prop.

12.2.2.head: الوَجناء
12.2.2.meaning: A tough camel, also associated with prominent cheekbones.

14.1.2.head: العيس
14.1.2.meaning: Light-coloured camels with a tawny tinge.

14.1.5-6.head: أَبو دُلَف
14.1.5-6.meaning: Abu Dulaf, al-Qasim ibn Isa al-Ijli, an Abbasid governor and commander.

15.2.1.head: تَمائِم
15.2.1.meaning: Amulets once tied to children for protection.

15.2.4.head: الذَّوائِب
15.2.4.meaning: Long or hanging locks of hair.

16.2.3.head: عَوَّذَ
16.2.3.meaning: To charm or protect by an invocation.

18.1.4.head: عِراص
18.1.4.meaning: The open courtyards of a settlement. The recited ṣād sounds close to an ordinary s.

19.2.1.head: هَدِيّ
19.2.1.meaning: A bride being escorted to her husband.

22.1.4.head: لُجَيم
22.1.4.meaning: Lujaym, an ancestor in Bakr ibn Wa'il. The patron’s tribe Ijl belonged to this line. The middle consonant sounds close to a z in the recitation.

22.2.1-2.head: بَنو الحِصن
22.2.1-2.meaning: Banu al-Hisn, descendants of Tha'laba ibn Ukaba of Bakr in al-Suli’s account. The name means “fortress” and echoes the word for the women of honour who bore them.

23.2.3.head: الرَّوع
23.2.3.meaning: Terror at the height of battle.

24.1.5.head: جَبرِيَّة
24.1.5.meaning: Haughtiness and a tyrant’s claim to power.

24.2.3.head: حَرَبَ
24.2.3.meaning: To plunder or strip someone of property.

25.1.5.head: عَواصِم
25.1.5.meaning: Giving protection to those who seek it.

26.1.4.head: قَسطَل
26.1.4.meaning: A dense cloud of battle dust.

26.2.2.meaning: The upper shafts or points of spears.

27.1.4.head: تَميم
27.1.4.meaning: Tamim, the tribe of Hajib, whose bow figures in the next bayt.

28.1.2-3.head: ذو قار
28.1.2-3.meaning: Dhu Qar, the Iraqi site of Bakr ibn Wa'il’s celebrated victory over Persian forces.

28.2.5.head: حاجِب
28.2.5.meaning: Hajib ibn Zurara, who in the famous account pledged his bow to the Persian king as security for his tribe.

31.1.3.head: الأَفشين
31.1.3.meaning: Al-Afshin, the title of Haydar ibn Kawus, al-Mu'tasim’s commander against Babak.

32.1.3.meaning: Grew pitch dark, here of a crisis.

33.1.1.head: تَجَلَّلَ
33.1.1.meaning: Rose over it and encompassed it.

34.1.1.head: أَرشَق
34.1.1.meaning: Arshaq, a place in the Azerbaijan campaign against Babak.

35.1.1.head: نَضا
35.1.1.meaning: Drew something from its sheath or cover.

36.2.1.head: ضَرائِب
36.2.1.meaning: Inborn qualities or traits of character.

37.2.2.meaning: Singled out for a distinction or preferred rank.

38.2.1.head: فَلَّ
38.2.1.meaning: To blunt an utterance or break its force.

40.1.2.head: أَراحَ
40.1.2.meaning: Brought livestock home in the evening.

40.1.3.head: عازِب
40.1.3.meaning: Ranging far away, as stock on distant pasture.

44.1.4.head: القاسِم
44.1.4.meaning: Al-Qasim, Abu Dulaf’s personal name, also suggesting the distributor of gifts.
